newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland agog at "murky business" in parliament.
newsitem.headline: Ireland agog at "murky business" in parliament.

text.p: Ireland's biggest department store chain said on Wednesday it would show tax inspectors a report which led to the resignation of a government minister and media reports of a million-pound payout to a leading political figure.

Dunnes Stores said in a brief statement that it would make the report available to the tax authorities after an appeal by Prime Minister John Bruton following the weekend resignation of Michael Lowry as transport minister.

Lowry, a young star within the ruling Fine Gael party, resigned abruptly on Saturday night after admitting that Dunnes Stores paid 200,000 punts ($330,000) for the extension and rennovation in 1992 of his private home in County Tipperary.
He was chairman of the party's parliamentary group at the time and head of his own company, which provided refrigeration systems for Dunnes Stores throughout the country.

The Irish Times said a report by a firm of chartered accounts showed that privately owned Dunnes Stores, which has clothing and food outlets on every major Irish urban shopping street, had made several similar payments.
It said one million Irish pounds went to a former government minister of the opposition Fianna Fail party,
Fianna Fail was in power until November two years ago when former prime minister Albert Reynolds resigned in a scandal over legal appointments and stepped down as party leader.
Fianna Fail's current leader, Bertie Ahern, told parliament on Tuesday night that he was satisfied none of the spokesmen in his party had received any payment whatsoever.
He called for the publication of the report. "It is in the public interest. We cannot have a dark cloud hanging over our public life," he said.
The issue has monopolised the airwaves and newspapers for days and the Dunnes report has been labelled the "Doomsday Book" by the media, which scents a major scandal in the offing.

The media has suggested that such payments may have been made without payment of tax or to win political favours. Lowry has denied any impropriety but has yet to explain fully how the country's biggest store ended up paying for work on his home.
"Rumours abound that other senior figures are implicated," the Irish Times said in an editorial entitled "Murky Business".
"All of this is contributing to something more than the usual public cynicism about politics and politicians and where they interact with business and business people," it said.

"There is a sense of unease that what has been revealed to date may be but the tip of an iceberg and that the political system, and more pertinently the relationship between politics and business, is deeply compromised," it said. (1=.6049 Punt)
